summary: For 9–10 year olds, teach air resistance as a resistive (frictional) force that acts opposite to an object's motion and grows with surface area and speed. The central corrective target is the misconception that all objects experience the same air resistance regardless of size or shape. A route well aligned with the curriculum combines a hands-on fair-test investigation using the same sheet of paper flat versus crumpled (so weight is held constant and area becomes the visible cause) with a live falling-object model, in which an upward resistance arrow grows as the object speeds up until it balances weight and the object then falls at a steady speed. Supporting retrieval (ordering by fall time, arrow-direction questions) and a static labelled force diagram serve as scaffolds, not replacements for the predict–measure experience.
misconceptions: All objects experience the same amount of air resistance regardless of size or shape (Oak-named misconception)
Air resistance acts in all directions, or acts downward — it is directional and acts opposite to motion
Air resistance is the same as 'wind'
Mass is irrelevant to falling — yet with air resistance present, two objects of the same shape but different mass do not fall identically
Heavier objects always fall faster (the Aristotelian carryover) — true-ish for same-shape objects in air, but it conflates air resistance with the underlying gravity story

activities.title: Growing resistance: drop and watch the arrows balance
steps: Build a falling object and use a slider to change its surface area — flatten a ball into a flat sheet, or widen a parachute canopy.
Drop it down a tall chute and watch the upward air-resistance arrow grow from nothing as the object speeds up.
Keep watching until the upward arrow matches the downward weight arrow and the object stops speeding up, then falls at a steady speed.

Widen the canopy and observe the arrows balancing sooner, at a lower speed (it floats gently); streamline it and observe the upward arrow growing more slowly, so the object reaches a much higher speed before the arrows balance (it plummets).
Use a 'fair test' mode to drop two objects differing in exactly one variable (e.g. surface area) and read the cause straight off the race.
activities.insight: Air resistance is not fixed: it grows with both speed and surface area, and always pushes back against the direction of motion. When it balances weight the object stops accelerating and falls at a steady speed (it keeps moving). Two shapes of the same weight are NOT slowed the same.

activities.title: Fair-test investigation: same paper, flat vs crumpled
steps: Predict first: drop a flat sheet of paper (held level, not edge-on) and the SAME sheet crumpled into a tight ball together from the same height — which lands first, and why? (Use two identical sheets, one flat and one crumpled, so both can be dropped at once.)
State the prediction and reason aloud or in writing BEFORE dropping.
Drop both and observe which lands first.
Weigh both to confirm they are identical in mass, so weight cannot explain the difference.
Repeat the drop several times and compare; extend to a big vs small parachute, taking repeat readings and recording fall times in a table.
activities.insight: Because the flat sheet and the crumpled ball are identical paper with the same weight, gravity pulls equally; the flat sheet meets MORE air because of its larger surface area facing the air, so it falls slower. At a given speed, the size of the air resistance depends on surface area and shape, not on the object's weight.

activities.title: Which way does it push? Direction and retrieval practice
steps: Order a set of parachutes/shapes by their fall time.
Answer which way air resistance pushes on a falling object — up, down, or sideways — and justify it.
Use a slider to explore how changing surface area changes fall time, predicting before each change.
Draw or complete a force diagram on a falling object showing weight down and air resistance opposing the motion (up for a falling object).
activities.insight: Air resistance acts opposite to the direction of movement — upward on a falling object — and larger area gives more resistance and a slower fall. It is not 'wind' and does not act in all directions.

activities.title: Connecting the ideas: parachutes, streamlining, water and the Moon
steps: Explain what a parachutist changes to slow down (area, not weight) when a big canopy opens.
Contrast maximising air resistance (parachutes) with minimising it (streamlined shapes).

Give an everyday example of water resistance and explain how it, like air resistance and surface friction, opposes motion; water and air resistance act on objects moving through water or air, while surface friction acts between surfaces in contact.
Predict what the flat sheet and the crumpled ball would do if dropped where there is no air at all (e.g. the Moon) and explain why.
activities.insight: Air resistance, water resistance and surface friction are all resistive forces that oppose motion. Air and water resistance can be increased (bigger area facing the air or water) or reduced (streamlining); surface friction depends mainly on how rough the surfaces are and how hard they press together. Without air (as on the Moon) there is no air resistance, so the paper ball and the flat sheet would land together.

checkQuestion: I drop a flat sheet of paper and, at the same moment, the SAME sheet screwed into a tight ball, from the same height. Which lands first — and why, given they're made of exactly the same paper and weigh the same?
checkAnswer: The screwed-up ball lands first. Both weigh the same, so gravity pulls equally, but the flat sheet has a much bigger surface facing the air, so it meets MORE air resistance pushing up against its fall — that slows it. Air resistance depends on surface area (and speed), not on weight; the ball has less area, so less air resistance.
